claims.text: Sustained oxidation resistance in NiCoCrFeAl-based multiprincipal-element alloys is governed by a transition between diffusion-limited and reaction-limited oxide-scale formation.
Alloy composition controls elemental diffusion kinetics during oxidation.
Alloy composition controls interfacial reaction rates during oxidation.
Elemental diffusion kinetics and interfacial reaction rates determine oxide-scale adhesion.
Elemental diffusion kinetics and interfacial reaction rates determine oxide-scale growth rate.
Elemental diffusion kinetics and interfacial reaction rates determine overall material integrity at high temperature.
Oxidation behavior is dictated by the interplay between metal-cation diffusion, oxygen-anion diffusion, and protective-oxide-forming interfacial reactions.
Composition changes shift the balance between diffusion-controlled growth and reaction-limited scale formation.
The balance between diffusion-controlled and reaction-limited oxidation influences scale integrity and spallation.
Oxide growth will initially follow diffusion-limited kinetics and later transition to reaction-limited behavior.
The proposed kinetic transition will produce predictable oxide-scale thickness patterns.
The proposed kinetic transition will produce predictable spallation patterns.
The hypothesis is expected to apply from 1000 to 1100 degrees Celsius under controlled oxygen partial pressures.
A reference NiCoCrFeAl alloy has well-established oxidation behavior documented in prior literature.
